rows.row: | PERC-01 | The gap between a label and its control is ≥ the gap to a neighbour, a redundant one-item group box implies a group, or a within-group gap equals or exceeds the surrounding between-group gap | **Proximity binds meaning**: place each label nearer its target than any distractor, keep within-group gaps smaller than the surrounding between-group gap, and remove redundant single-item group boxes; otherwise spacing or boxes create false associations (Gestalt proximity) (↔ design [[LAY-03]](design-aesthetics.md#lay-03) designs unequal intervals as rhythm; this row checks whether spacing depicts the intended group boundaries) | Do labels, gaps, and any remaining group boxes depict the intended associations without redundant single-item boxes? | S·r | [Designing with the Mind in Mind](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-with-the-mind-in-mind) + [Refactoring UI, § avoid-ambiguous-spacing](../SOURCES.md#src-refactoring-ui) |

| PERC-03 | A finished layout claims a multi-element grouping | **Seven-principle Gestalt audit**: before shipping a grouped display, check proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, symmetry, figure-ground, and common-fate for relations you did not intend (↔ grph [[GRPH-22]](graph-theory.md#grph-22), eng [[DOM-03]](engineering.md#dom-03); ↔ [[HAI-05]](interaction-ux.md#hai-05) a perceived autonomy boundary the system does not hold; ↔ [[SEC-01]](security.md#sec-01) trust changes at every crossing so an unenforced boundary is only in the mind; ↔ [[CLM-03]](business-marketing.md#clm-03) a policy promise against a divergent implementation; ↔ [[WEB-08]](security.md#web-08) route check without object auth is a boundary the eye trusts and the server does not) | Does any Gestalt principle invent a relation we don't mean? | S·r | [Designing with the Mind in Mind](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-with-the-mind-in-mind) |

| PERC-07 | A strong interrupt (modal, blink, beep, confirm) fires on a high-frequency path | **Don't habituate alarms**: reserve strong attention-getting methods for rare, critical, irreversible events and suppress the routine, or users learn to dismiss the one that matters (↔ [[HAI-13]](interaction-ux.md#hai-13) the AI-verify-cue instance: a standing "verify" cue on every fluent output is the alarm that habituates, so the last error detector goes quiet; ↔ eng [[OBS-04]](engineering.md#obs-04) a signal that always fires goes quiet in the reader, [[AGT-16]](engineering.md#agt-16) constant confirmation trains the reflex press) | Is this interrupt rarer and worse than the routine noise around it? | B·p | [Designing with the Mind in Mind](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-with-the-mind-in-mind) |

| NAV-05 | Top-level nav labels have overlapping homes or a live task with no home | **MECE categories**: make primary categories mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive; a dual-home or a gap means the user cannot choose where to look or file (↔ grph [[GRPH-22]](graph-theory.md#grph-22); ↔ [[CLM-03]](business-marketing.md#clm-03) policy text and implementation must share one home; ↔ [[TEAM-01]](planning.md#team-01) an architectural split the org does not communicate across is a boundary only on the diagram) | Can every in-scope item name exactly one primary nav home? | S·p | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| NAV-11 | A shareable or restorable view (map, filter, doc) does not round-trip through the URL | **Deep Links encode place and state**: put location and critical view params in the URL (excluding preference-stomping state), or the view cannot be shared or restored | Does opening the URL restore the same place and view? | S·w | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| INT-05 | The final commit is a link, low-contrast, far from the last field, or a peer of secondaries | **Prominent Done**: the final commit is one unmistakable button with a verb label at the end of the flow near the last control, or users abandon or pick the wrong next step | Is there one unmistakable final action after the last input? | S·r | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| INT-07 | A heavyweight, costly, or hard-to-predict action commits with no outcome sample | **Preview before commit**: when cost or unpredictability is high, show the outcome with commit and back-out on the same surface (↔ [Principle 13]; ↔ [[COG-04]](interaction-ux.md#cog-04) compute the comparison for the deliberate mind before a high-stakes choice; ↔ [[CLM-05]](business-marketing.md#clm-05) the hostile reader must check the claim before it ships; ↔ [[STRAT-02]](business-marketing.md#strat-02) name the disconfirmers before the forward plan) | Can the user see the result before they pay / print / apply? | B·p | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| INT-08 | An operation runs longer than ~1s with no progress, or a long job has no cancel | **Wait state and cancel**: over ~1s show progress (a meter if the duration is known); over ~2s and interruptible, offer a side-effect-free Cancel, or users double-submit or abandon (↔ eng [[API-07]](engineering.md#api-07) 202 + poll/cancel resource; ↔ a11y [[A11Y-21]](accessibility.md#a11y-21) announce status) | If delay exceeds ~1s, is status or progress shown, and if an interruptible operation lasts >~2s, is side-effect-free Cancel beside the indicator? | B·w | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| INT-09 | An editor mutates data with no multilevel undo stack | **Reversible command stack**: model discrete, user-named changes as reversible LIFO operations, keep at least 10–12 recent items where feasible, and extend the history when observation or usability testing justifies it; exclude pure navigation and view changes, because safe recovery lets users explore without treating edits as permanent (↔ [Principle 3] reversible history supports the safe exploration this principle asks for; ↔ [[HAI-02]](interaction-ux.md#hai-02) a correction must reach its source before a later recompute; ↔ [[DATA-14]](engineering.md#data-14) patch the single authority instead of a divergent copy; ↔ [[HITL-01]](ml-systems.md#hitl-01) close the loop so the next training run consumes the correction; ↔ [[AIPX-03]](business-marketing.md#aipx-03) production use becomes the feedback label source; ↔ [[SERVE-04]](ml-systems.md#serve-04) correct the source rather than frozen-model postprocessing) | Can the user undo the last N permanent-ish edits? | B·p | [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed.](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) + [Designing Interfaces, 3rd ed., ch. 8](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-interfaces) |

| INT-10 | AI or automation mutates content or state with no status, predictable next step, or stop | **Status–predict–stop**: automated action exposes its status, the predictable next step, and a cancel/undo; prefer an optional suggestion over a silent auto-commit, or the user cannot intervene (↔ [[HAI-04]](interaction-ux.md#hai-04) for AI effectors) | Can the user see state, predict the next action, and stop it? | B·w | [Human-Centered AI](../SOURCES.md#src-human-centered-ai) |

| INT-16 | A pause or interruption can drop the goal, a completed step, or the current state of a multi-step activity before the user returns. | **Resume from preserved state**: keep the goal, the progress, and the state needed to re-enter, using cues or a checklist that tracks required items without imposing a sequence the work does not have, because reconstructing the task from memory skips or repeats steps. ↔ [[COG-01]](interaction-ux.md#cog-01) show residue when a flow holds more than a few novel items off-screen; this row is the residue that must survive a pause. ↔ [[INT-11]](interaction-ux.md#int-11) keep a good generated prefix; this row keeps ordinary task state across an interruption. | Can the user resume without rebuilding the prior goal and state from memory? | S·w | [The Design of Everyday Things, ch. 5](../SOURCES.md#src-design-of-everyday-things-norman) |

| LAY-01 | all blocks carry equal visual weight | **Contrast engine / big-little law**: hierarchy via size, weight, position, silhouette; one dominant (↔ ux [[PERC-06]](interaction-ux.md#perc-06) without a dominant the eye searches linearly) | What must dominate, and what is subdued? | S·l | [Asymmetric Typography (Jan Tschichold), § use-of-space](../SOURCES.md#src-asymmetric-typography) |

| LAY-03 | identical gaps between all content groups | **Unequal intervals**: spacing differentiates relatedness and creates tension (↔ ux [[PERC-01]](interaction-ux.md#perc-01) within-group gaps stay smaller than between-group gaps to preserve relatedness; this rule sets the typographic rhythm) | Do intervals encode relatedness? | S·l | [Asymmetric Typography (Jan Tschichold), § use-of-space](../SOURCES.md#src-asymmetric-typography) |

| LAY-06 | hierarchy depends on boxes and rules | **Hierarchy without ornament**: weight/size/position carry meaning; frames are a crutch (↔ ux [[VIZ-02]](interaction-ux.md#viz-02) rank the critical channel before decoration) | If ornament vanished, would hierarchy remain? | S·l | [Asymmetric Typography (Jan Tschichold), § decorative-typography](../SOURCES.md#src-asymmetric-typography) |

| DATA-14 | Code writes the same logical change to two stores (DB + index/cache) | **No dual writes**: without a single order authority the copies diverge permanently and silently; derive the second from the first's change log (↔ ux [[HAI-02]](interaction-ux.md#hai-02) a human edit that skips the underlying model returns after recompute; ↔ ml [[HITL-01]](ml-systems.md#hitl-01) retrain on the correction or the same error is re-served; ↔ ux [[INT-09]](interaction-ux.md#int-09) the edit is a reversible op on real data, not a cosmetic overwrite; ↔ writ [[WRIT-44]](writing.md#writ-44) swapping the flagged phrase while leaving the defect intact only launders the tell; ↔ biz [[AIPX-03]](business-marketing.md#aipx-03) production accept/edit must feed the next training source) | Which system is the system of record? | B·p | [Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 11](../SOURCES.md#src-designing-data-intensive-applications) |

| TEST-22 | Separate component pipelines are green, and no integration run has recorded the exact component versions that were assembled together | **Test the assembled version tuple**: keep each component's tested binary and source identity in an artifact repository, assemble the selected versions, run whole-application checks, and record that version tuple, because a green component does not prove the composition works (↔ [[RLSE-12]](engineering.md#rlse-12) green must mean the deployable unit, not a later integration still to do; ↔ [[TEST-10]](engineering.md#test-10) an end-to-end suite is a supplement and does not by itself record this tuple; ↔ [[TEST-27]](engineering.md#test-27) probe old and new peers that actually meet in production) | Which exact component versions passed the whole-application checks together? | S·r | [Continuous Delivery, ch. 13](../SOURCES.md#src-continuous-delivery-humble-farley) |

| GRPH-01 | Plan has ordered steps, build targets, migrations, or module dependencies | **Model the work as a DAG, then topological-sort**: only a directed *acyclic* dependency graph yields a legal execution order; sequence invented by gut invents illegal ones (↔ eng [[DATA-15]](engineering.md#data-15) order from the causal structure, not wall-clock or gut) | What are the nodes, the directed edges, and the proven acyclic order? | S·p | [The Algorithm Design Manual, ch. 7](../SOURCES.md#src-algorithm-design-manual) |

| GRPH-09 | Scheduling jobs, or allocating locks/registers/rooms with pairwise conflicts | **Colour the conflict graph**: the chromatic number is the minimum resources for a conflict-free assignment, and the largest clique is a hard lower bound on it | What is the conflict graph, and can it be coloured with the resources you have? | S·p | [Graph Theory with Applications, ch. 8](../SOURCES.md#src-graph-theory-with-applications) |

| GRPH-31 | A set of tasks with dependencies must run across workers, threads, or lanes and the schedule or degree of parallelism is being guessed, or precedence-graph width is used as simultaneous admission capacity | **Critical-path schedule the task DAG**: with unlimited workers, the critical path is the makespan floor; in topological order, start each job when its latest prerequisite completes. Precedence-graph width counts the largest mutually unconstrained job set; it describes logical independence, so bound simultaneous launches separately by measured workers, memory, and co-tenant capacity. With a finite worker count and arbitrary precedence, makespan is strongly NP-hard; for unit-time jobs with tree precedence, the Critical Path (CP) rule prioritizes a ready job at the head of the longest string (↔ [[GRPH-01]](graph-theory.md#grph-01) the DAG is the substrate this schedules over; ↔ [[GRPH-09]](graph-theory.md#grph-09) pairwise interference without precedence is the sibling colouring structure, not this; ↔ [[PERF-04]](engineering.md#perf-04) the DAG's serial spine still caps speedup by Amdahl). | What is the unlimited-worker critical-path floor, and when can each job start? If width sets the launch count, what measured workers, memory, and co-tenant capacity bound simultaneous admission? Is finite-worker precedence arbitrary, or unit-time tree, and which CP priority applies? | S·p | [The Algorithm Design Manual, ch. 17](../SOURCES.md#src-algorithm-design-manual) + [Scheduling: Theory, Algorithms, and Systems, ch. 5](../SOURCES.md#src-pinedo-scheduling) + [Scheduling: Theory, Algorithms, and Systems, §D.4](../SOURCES.md#src-pinedo-scheduling) |

| GRPH-32 | An agent pipeline whose steps are chained by "and then" with no data passed between them | **An edge exists only where data moves**: when a step is sequenced after another, require that the downstream node actually read a named field of the upstream node's output, and delete the arrow when no such field can be named, because arrows inherited from typing order serialize independent work for nothing (↔ eng [[DATA-15]](engineering.md#data-15) order from the causal structure, not wall-clock or gut; ↔ [[GRPH-01]](graph-theory.md#grph-01) toposort only after the edges are real). Exempt: arrows required for side-effect order, resource exclusivity, rate limits, or idempotency even when no data field is read — name the non-data constraint instead of deleting the edge. | For this arrow, which field of the previous output does the next node read? | S·p | [bootstrap](../SOURCES.md#src-bootstrap) |

sections:
## Named mechanism: **Action Panel**
- **Source claim:** Always-visible (or sticky) free-form command surface more discoverable than hidden menus; place near target; dynamic by selection/state; closable panels need easy reopen if sole home of actions (ch8 *Action Panel*; Fig 8-6–8-8).
- **Observable trigger:** Many item/list actions only in right-click/menu with low discoverability; or panel far from operated objects.
- **Required action:** Surface high-frequency/relevant verbs in panel adjacent to targets; keep panel contents state-synced to selection.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Users never find commands; wrong association of verb to noun.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Small-screen density limits (source: not usually good for small devices); expert menu-bar apps with strong keyboard discoverability.
- **Verification recipe:** static screenshot · task test (first-use find-action)

## Named mechanism: **Prominent “Done” Button** / **Assumed Next Step**
- **Source claim:** Final commit of transaction/settings is a button (not link), strong treatment, label = user verb (Send/Buy/Install), placed at end of eye/task travel near last field (ch8 pattern; Fig 8-9–8-13). Secondary actions de-emphasized (ch10 forms cross-ref).
- **Observable trigger:** Submit is a link or low-contrast control; or Done far from last input; multiple equal-weight CTAs at commit step.
- **Required action:** One primary commit control at sequence end; verb label; secondary actions visually subordinate.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Abandoned purchase/form; “what next?” search; accidental secondary action.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Multi-primary marketing pages (still differentiate hierarchy); wizard intermediate Next vs final Purchase.
- **Verification recipe:** static screenshot · task test (completion path)

## Named mechanism: **Smart Menu Items**
- **Source claim:** Menu/button labels dynamically name the object/operation (“Undo Increase Clarity”, “Add [person] to Contacts”); disable when no object (ch8 *Smart Menu Items*; Fig 8-14 Lightroom, 8-15 Gmail).
- **Observable trigger:** Generic “Delete”/“Undo”/“Add to contacts” with ambiguous multi-object context; enabled with empty selection.
- **Required action:** Interpolate concrete target into label; disable when no valid target; plurals for multi-select.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Wrong-object destructive action; users stop exploring.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Extremely short mobile toolbars where space forces icons + tooltip only—still need confirm/preview for high cost.
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test (selection changes label)

## Named mechanism: **Preview**
- **Source claim:** Before heavyweight/costly/hard-to-predict action, show sample outcome + commit + back-out/change from preview (ch8 *Preview*; Fig 8-16–8-18). Opposite of “activate then wait to see.”
- **Observable trigger:** Purchase, print, large open, irreversible filter/transform, multi-step form submit with no summary/WYSIWYG sample.
- **Required action:** Show outcome summary/visual before commit; allow commit and back-out from same surface.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Costly errors; support load; distrust of filters/transforms.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Instant, free, fully reversible micro-edits with multilevel undo; pure navigation.
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test · task test

## Named mechanism: **Spinners and Loading Indicators** (+ Norman/Nielsen latency bands)
- **Source claim:** After submit, if response delayed: spinner (stateless) or loading indicator (proportion, remaining time, cancel). Bands: <0.1s live; 0.1–1s notice but wait; >1s risk “broken”—indicator mandatory (ch8 *Spinners…*; Fig 8-19–8-23). Prefer keep UI alive; place cancel near indicator.
- **Observable trigger:** Operation >~1s with frozen UI and no progress/spinner; or long job with spinner only when meter data available.
- **Required action:** Show status + progress when known; spinner when unknown; do not lock UI if avoidable; surface cancel collocated.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Double-submit, abandon, “hung” reports.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Sub-100ms interactions (no chrome); background jobs with separate notification channel if primary UI stays responsive and status is findable.
- **Verification recipe:** runtime metric (latency) · state-transition test

## Named mechanism: **Cancelability**
- **Source claim:** Instant cancel of long op with no side effects; Stop/Cancel + stop icon; confirm cancel worked ≤~1–2s; label which op when parallel (ch8 *Cancelability*; Fig 8-24–8-25). Supports **Safe Exploration**.
- **Observable trigger:** Modal/long job >~2s without cancel; cancel leaves partial writes; cancel >2s to acknowledge.
- **Required action:** Provide cancel; roll back or never commit partial; acknowledge immediately; disambiguate multi-job cancel.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Forced wait; stuck partial state; users fear exploration.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Truly atomic remote commits already completed (show undo/reverse path instead); non-interruptible hardware ops—still show honest “cannot cancel” state.
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test · runtime metric

## Named mechanism: **Multilevel Undo** / **reversible operations** / **action history stack**
- **Source claim:** Model actions as discrete, named, reversible ops; stack LIFO ≥10–12; undo permanent-ish changes (edit, delete, layout, paste); do not put navigation/selection/scroll/window chrome on stack; impossible undos (sent mail, forum post, purchase) must be obvious (ch8 *Multilevel Undo*; Fig 8-26). Hard to retrofit—architecture first.
- **Observable trigger:** Highly interactive editor/mail/graphics app with only single-level undo or none; irreversible file/object deletes without undo; undo labeled generically without next op (tie to Smart Menu Items).
- **Required action:** Implement reversible command model + multilevel stack + smart undo labels; exclude pure view/nav from stack.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Fear of exploration; catastrophic recovery (reload/backup); creative flow broken.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Simple form/nav apps; external side effects that cannot reverse—use Preview/confirm + compensating action instead of false Undo.
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test · task test (N undos)

## Named mechanism: **MECE** (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive)
- **Source claim:** Categories must be clearly distinct (no confusing overlap) and together complete for intended content + use cases; expandable without confusion; categories become nav foundation (ch2 “Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive”; site maps/content outlines as docs).
- **Observable trigger:** Nav/sitemap labels where same item fits two top-level buckets, or a supported task/object has no home; ambiguous mega-menu cells.
- **Required action:** Rewrite taxonomy so each item has one primary home; every in-scope content/task maps to a place; document with site map/outline.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Users can’t decide where to look/put things; nav feels arbitrary; growth breaks structure (ch2 MECE).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Secondary associative paths (tags, related content, search hits) may multi-link; **MECE** binds the *primary* organization scheme, not every cross-link.
- **Verification recipe:** static sitemap audit — sample N objects/tasks; each has exactly one primary path + ≥1 path for every in-scope case.

## Named mechanism: **Frequency of use** (visibility by demand)
- **Source claim:** Frequent tasks/controls/topics must be immediately available without search/browse; rare items may be buried (settings, help) (ch2 “Make Frequently Used Items Visible”). Ch3: elevate frequent actions into top-level **global navigation** independent of formal hierarchy depth; bury infrequent behind submenu/accordion/tab (ch3 “Put frequently accessed items directly in the global navigation”).
- **Observable trigger:** High-use action (analytics/task list) requires multi-level drill while rare settings share equal prominence; global nav reflects org chart not use frequency.
- **Required action:** Rank by expected frequency; promote top-N to always-visible global/primary chrome; demote low-N behind progressive disclosure.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Everyday work costs repeated search/browse; experts still pay novice path cost.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Safety/legal items may need high visibility despite low frequency; expert **accelerators** (shortcuts) complement but don’t replace visible frequent paths for mixed audiences (ch2 novice/experienced).
- **Verification recipe:** task test / runtime metric — top tasks ≤ target clicks/taps vs baseline; rare settings ≥1 extra disclosure step.

## Named mechanism: **Context-switch cost** + **keep distances short**
- **Source claim:** Opening page/window incurs cognitive cost (reorient shape/layout/exits); even familiar pages cost; load latency reduces exploration — “latency costs viewers” (ch3 Cognitive Load). Minimize taps/clicks A→B: broad top-level (flatten hierarchy), put frequent items in global nav, bring common tasks onto one screen — aim most common ~80% use cases one page without context switches; avoid multi-page simple tasks especially with step dependencies (ch3 Keep Distances Short + subsections). Multilevel tree needs ≥2 jumps subpage→subpage; convert toward fully-connected via **Fat Menus** / **Sitemap Footer** (ch3 Multilevel or Tree; Fat Menus/Sitemap Footer Why).
- **Observable trigger:** Common task needs many routes/dialogs; deep tree without full cross-links; top nav only 2–3 items forcing long cascade; measured multi-hop for high-frequency paths.
- **Required action:** Flatten/broaden primary nav; co-locate dependent steps; convert multilevel to single-jump reachability for major pages (fat menu or sitemap footer) when hierarchy is deep.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Accumulated reorientation + wasted backtracks on missing preconditions; abandoned slow pages (ch3).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Focused modes (fullscreen slideshow) should *strip* global nav — short distance ≠ always show everything; use Back/Next + **Escape Hatch** (ch3 Flat Navigation note on modes). Hub-and-spoke mobile when spokes can’t fit full global nav (ch3 Hub and Spoke).
- **Verification recipe:** runtime metric / task test — hop count for top tasks; max depth of primary IA; major pages reachable in ≤1 jump from any major page if claiming fully-connected.

## Named mechanism: **Clear Entry Points**
- **Source claim:** Few main entry “doors,” task- or audience-oriented, clear CTAs; first-time/infrequent users; smaller specialized links must not out-compete front doors (ch3 Clear Entry Points What/How; Fig 3-7). Skip if purpose already clear and extra step would irritate intermediates/experts.
- **Observable trigger:** First screen is dense undifferentiated chrome/ads/disabled toolbars with no primary start tasks; or many equal-weight doors.
- **Required action:** 1–few dominant, plain-language entry actions covering most arrival goals; demote secondary nav visually.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** “OK, here I am. Now what?” — hesitant users don’t begin (ch3 Why).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Expert-first tools where extra entry step is pure friction (ch3 Use when).
- **Verification recipe:** static screenshot + first-run task test — new users pick correct start without hunting.

## Named mechanism: **Escape Hatch**
- **Source claim:** Well-labeled control from limited-nav screens (wizard, **Modal Panel**, deep-link landing, error/dead-end) back to safe known place (home/hub/full-nav) (ch3 Escape Hatch; wayfinding “trump card”). Supports safe exploration; prevents app abandon; logo-home, Cancel as hatch (How/Examples).
- **Observable trigger:** Modal/wizard/error/SERP-landed page with no path to full-nav hub; trapped serial flow without cancel/home.
- **Required action:** Always-visible labeled hatch to safe place on limited-nav and error screens; deep-link targets must include hatch (Why).
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Felt trap → hard exit (close app); can’t recover from wrong branch/deep link (ch3).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Fully-connected pages already showing global nav (hatch redundant as separate control; home logo still fine).
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test — from modal/wizard/404/deep-link, one control returns to hub with full nav.

## Named mechanism: **Breadcrumbs** (hierarchy context) vs **Progress Indicator** (linear map)
- **Source claim:** **Breadcrumbs** = parent–child slice of IA hierarchy — “you are here” relative to site, *not* click-history; essential after search/faceted/deep-link landings when global nav can’t show deep position (ch3 Breadcrumbs What/Why; Target Fig 3-55). **Progress Indicator** = map of linear sequence with you-are-here (+ optional jump back); for Wizard/narrative/process; shows remaining work; hierarchical topology → breadcrumbs instead (ch3 Progress Indicator Use when/Why/How).
- **Observable trigger:** Hierarchy depth ≥2 without breadcrumb trail; linear checkout/wizard without step map; breadcrumbs used as Back-stack history only; progress map without titles when steps differ in kind.
- **Required action:** Deep hierarchical/content IA → **Breadcrumbs** (titles as links up). Linear prescribed process → **Progress Indicator** with current/done states and short step titles (numbers alone weak).
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Deep-landed users lack context (breadcrumbs) or can’t estimate finish / re-enter prior step (progress) (ch3).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Flat 1-level sites; pure tool **flat navigation**; tiny 2-step flows may skip full map if remaining work is obvious (still show step identity).
- **Verification recipe:** screenshot + deep-link task — land mid-tree via search; breadcrumb shows path; wizard shows remaining steps accurately.

## Named mechanism: **Deep Links** (location + state in URL)
- **Source claim:** Persist location *and* relevant app state in URL/bookmarkable link (position, layers, zoom, etc.); reload restores; shareable; mobile app-to-app without losing task context (ch3 Deep Links). Don’t capture settings that would stomp user prefs — scenario-design what belongs in link (How).
- **Observable trigger:** Interactive content (map, document page, filtered results, multi-step mid-flow) with non-shareable/ephemeral state; refresh loses place; no permalink control.
- **Required action:** Encode restorable position+chosen view state in URL; document which state is linkable vs session-local.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Forced multi-hop re-find; can’t share exact view; mobile context loss (ch3 Why).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Private/security-sensitive state must not go in URL; pure ephemeral drafts may stay session-only.
- **Verification recipe:** state-transition test — copy URL, new session/device restores intended view without re-traversing IA.

## Named mechanism: **Modal Panel** (forced focus) + **Animated Transition** (orientation under change)

## Named mechanism: **Goal-filtered perception** (scan, not read)
- **Source claim:** Goals **guide** sampling and **filter** preconscious notice; unrelated items often never register (scissors task; Canterbury “win $100” missed). Adults more goal-filtered than children. Ch1 “Perception Biased by Goals,” Figs 1.8–1.9, pp. 8–12; takeaways.
- **Observable trigger:** Plan/copy assumes users “will see” banner, promo, side-nav, or secondary legal text while pursuing unrelated primary goal; success path relies on non-goal-aligned chrome.
- **Required action:** Map each step’s user goal; place needed info/actions **goal-scented** (labels match goal words), prominent on path; never sole-path on goal-orthogonal chrome.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** High miss rate on “obvious” elements; support tickets “feature missing.”
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Exploration/browsing tasks without sharp goal; training modes that force full scan.
- **Verification recipe:** Task test with assigned goal + free report of non-goal elements. Eye-tracking optional.

## Named mechanism: **Gestalt proximity**
- **Source claim:** Relative distance drives perceived subgroups; near objects group even if dissimilar. Prefer spacing over group-boxes; label–control gap must bind correct pair (Delta vs United radios). Ch2 Proximity, Figs 2.1–2.5, pp. 16–18.
- **Observable trigger:** Label closer to neighbor control than own; form sections use boxes for single control; related controls spaced like unrelated.
- **Required action:** Encode intended groups by spacing hierarchy first; label closer to target than to distractors; remove redundant single-item group boxes.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Wrong radio selected; users can’t find which label maps which field.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Dense data tables where grid lines are the structure (still verify cell-label binding); a11y still needs programmatic association.
- **Verification recipe:** Static screenshot — measure label–control vs label–neighbor distances. DOM: `label[for]` matches visual proximity.

## Named mechanism: **Gestalt similarity**
- **Source claim:** Similar appearance → perceived group (bold unread mail; car-shape rides). Unintended similarity creates false groups (two similar menus). Ch2 Similarity, Figs 2.6–2.8, pp. 18–20.
- **Observable trigger:** Same style on unrelated actions; critical status not uniquely styled; parallel widgets look identical but mean different things.
- **Required action:** Shared look only for shared semantics; status/unread/availability via consistent distinctive feature; break false groups by differentiation.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Users treat unrelated controls as one set; miss status that doesn’t pop.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Brand-uniform chrome where all chrome is non-semantic; intentional monochrome systems using position alone (then proximity must carry load).
- **Verification recipe:** Static screenshot Gestalt audit: list perceived groups vs intended.

## Named mechanism: **Gestalt continuity / closure / symmetry / common fate / figure–ground**
- **Source claim:** Alignment fills gaps into continuous forms (sliders, IBM logo); incomplete figures close (stacks); complex scenes simplify to symmetric wholes (tables); co-motion groups; smaller/overlapping = figure. Combined principles can imply **unintended** relations — audit all seven. Ch2 Continuity–Common Fate + Combined, Figs 2.9–2.23, pp. 20–29.
- **Observable trigger:** Aligned but unrelated elements; partial stack implying more items than exist; animated co-motion of unrelated entities; modal/overlay without clear figure elevation; table-less prose for comparable multi-attribute data.
- **Required action:** Align only related; stack affordance only if collection real; co-animate only related; overlays as temporary figure over preserved ground; comparable data in symmetric table structure.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** False continuity/group; users invent objects/relations not in data; lose place after replace-not-overlay.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Decorative motion with no semantic claim; intentionally abstract art UI.
- **Verification recipe:** Static screenshot Gestalt checklist (7 principles). Animation: common-fate audit. DOM for heading/table structure.

## Named mechanism: **Preview first, select and initiate, then manage execution** (+ predictive planning displays)
- **Source claim:** HCAI pattern 2 (Table 9.2; ch9): for temporal/robot processes—**preview** entire process, user selects plan, initiates, then **manages execution**. Navigation tools, cameras. Mercedes parking assist step-by-step intended actions; better: show expected path; Brooks & Szafir: **predictive planning displays** → higher accuracy + satisfaction (ch8).
- **Observable trigger:** Multi-step automated plan (drive path, robot trajectory, batch irreversible ops, agent tool chain) that starts without preview of intended steps/path and without mid-execution manage/cancel.
- **Required action:** Before commit: show plan/path/preview; require select/initiate; during: live status + modify/cancel; prefer predictive spatial/step display over opaque “working…”.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** User cannot accept/reject plan; surprise actuations; lower task accuracy and trust (ch8).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Single reversible keystroke autocomplete fully ignorable (Ex 9.5–9.6); sub-second hard-real-time safety actuation (airbag)—preview impossible; use pre-certified behavior + post-event log.
- **Verification recipe:** Screenshot of preview; state-transition: preview → initiate → manage → complete/cancel; task test accuracy with vs without preview.

## Named mechanism: **Interactive control panels** (steer; immediate feedback)
- **Source claim:** News recommender: three sliders; list updates **immediately** as users move them → more clicks + strong desire for control (ch6). Pattern 3: **Steer by way of interactive control panels** (Table 9.2; ch9). Thermostat: see state, reset, hear/see system respond, see goal achieved (Ex 9.1; ch9). Golden Rules: informative feedback; keep users in control (Table 9.1).
- **Observable trigger:** Preference/automation parameters exist only as one-shot config or black-box personalization with no live steering UI; or control change without visible system response.
- **Required action:** For preference-shaped AI, provide interactive controls (sliders/toggles/panels) with **immediate** result update; always show current state + that intent was recognized.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Users stuck with opaque recommendations; lower engagement/acceptance; false “automation vs augmentation” choice (ch9 Google guidebook critique).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Controls that are pure noise for the task (ch6: poorly designed unused controls ≠ argument against good ones); latency-bound batch jobs—show queued state + ETA, not fake instant.
- **Verification recipe:** DOM: controls bound to result region; task test: change control → result changes without page-rebuild dead-end; screenshot before/after slider.

## Named mechanism: **Interlocks, guards, and safe defaults**
- **Source claim:** Interlocks/guards prevent deadly mistakes (oven door, reverse thrusters only after touchdown, positive train control) (ch8). Excessive human control via complex panels + **unsafe defaults** is design failure, not “user error” (Thimbleby IV overdose—ch8). PCA: patient trigger *plus* lockout/total-dose interlocks; upper-right adds ML dosing + explanation + hospital monitoring (Figs 8.6–8.8; ch8). Formal methods / range checks generalize guards (ch8).
- **Observable trigger:** Destructive or clinical automation with defaults that select high-risk options; missing range locks; human can command physically impossible/unsafe state; or “user control” UI with no safety envelope.
- **Required action:** Safe-by-default settings; hard interlocks on impossible/unsafe commands; allow user control *inside* envelope; document lockout reasons in UI.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Deadly “human error” that is design failure; or excessive automation without envelope (MAX); or excessive unconstrained control (medication overdose).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Mastery activities where error is part of learning (upper-left: bike, piano—ch8)—soft guards only; emergency break-glass with audit (hospital drive / firefighter elevator keys—ch6, ch8).
- **Verification recipe:** State-transition: unsafe command rejected; default path = safe; review of default config values against hazard analysis.

## Named mechanism: **Comprehensible, predictable, controllable** interfaces (status → mental model → stop)
- **Source claim:** Successful designs are **comprehensible, predictable, and controllable**, raising self-efficacy → reliable/safe/trustworthy (ch9). Users adopt tech that shows **current status** on a control panel, supports a **mental model to predict future actions**, allows **stop** of unintelligible actions (ch7). Eight Golden Rules still apply to HCAI (Table 9.1). Non-intrusive optional AI: red squiggle / translation choices leave user deciding if/when to accept (Ex 9.5–9.6; ch9). Visual UIs that prevent/reduce need for post-hoc explainability (ch7).
- **Observable trigger:** AI feature changes state with no status indicator, no predictable next-step cue, no cancel; or auto-applies irreversible edits without optional accept; or “explainability” only as post-hoc essay with no live status/control.
- **Required action:** For each AI action: show state, make next action predictable, provide stop/undo; prefer optional suggestions over silent auto-commit for reversible content work.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Deskilling + surprise automation; users cannot intervene; trustworthiness perceived as magic not control (ch8 vigilance/deskilling).
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Auto-save of drafts with undo history is OK; silent auto-send/delete/deploy is not. Full computer autonomy region only when pre-justified rapid-action (Fig 8.3).
- **Verification recipe:** Screenshot status + next-step; state-transition stop/undo; task test: user predicts next automation step before it runs.

## ch-5 — The contrast engine (size, weight, position, silhouette) {#ch-5}

**Master law:** the strongest effect of any typographic design is when **contrasts are most clearly defined**. Significance of contrast is the basis of all modern designing.

**Contrast dimensions (compositional):**

| Dimension | Weak (anti) | Strong (prefer) |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Adjacent sizes too close (e.g. 9/10, 14/16) | Clear steps; limit families of sizes |
| Weight | Unity-of-type grey; one weight only | Semi-bold / bold / light as hierarchy (not letter-spacing) |
| Position | Everything centred or edge-aligned by habit | Off-centre, unequal margins, intentional opposition |
| Silhouette | Repetition of same shape | Long after short; single-line group next to 2–3 line group |
| Density | Even grey | Closely knit vs loosely knit parts — **tension** |
| Form family | Random mixes; shaded 3D types | Planned mixtures within limits (ch-10) |

**Avoid repetition or similarity of silhouette.** If top has a one-line group, next group should prefer two or three lines. Long shapes followed by short; heavy by light.

**Tension, not accident:** intervals and positions intentional. Absolute weight of contrasts is less important than the **tension they create**.

**Visiting-card micro-lesson:** an ordinary centred card is neutral, expresses nothing; place the name **off-centre** and the reader experiences new form — becomes aware white space plays a part, that proportion and contrast are being used.

**Double contrasts:** heavy rules with light types; large spaces between long and short lines; reverse (white on black) against normal black on white; boxed vs ragged groups; circle-isolated unit vs free groups.

**Cap on complexity:** too many units cannot be absorbed at a glance. Prefer **three groups** (ch-8). Six type styles in one job is a hard upper bound and should be rare.

↔ eng UI: do not import this as “always bigger = primary button hierarchy only.” Here contrast is **full-page composition**, including position and white mass.

## ch-8 — Grouping: three units, unequal intervals, sense order {#ch-8}

**Grouping is new relative to conventional loose connection of parts.** Modern reading needs quick, exact transfer of words — sharp distinctions by sense.

| Rule | Spec |
|---|---|
| Default group count | **Three** groups |
| Two groups | Only very short, simple copy |
| Four groups | Only very long copy — four already requires counting |
| Comprehension test | Groups defeat purpose if they must be counted rather than absorbed at a glance |
| Separation | Each unit distinct; coherence not spoiled by a neighbour too close |
| Sequence | Placement below/beside follows **common sense of reading order** |
| Intervals | Unequal; sense-coherent; related to internal leading |

**Line length in multi-line headings (sense first):** length depends on sense and reading pauses, not decorative equal lengths. First line may be longer or shorter than second. Avoid word breaks. **Equal-length lines in a heading** — even accidental — are unsightly; fix with slight spacing change; never introduce intentionally for decorative block look.

**Words connected by sense** stay together even in large titles (“The New Typography” not “The New / Typography” when avoidable).

**Indentation (paragraph articulation):**

- Full-out-left headings do **not** imply abolishing paragraph indents.
- Indent (~1 em, more for very long heavily leaded lines) is best technical and aesthetic paragraph mark.
- No indent at chapter start if unnecessary; no indent when blank line separates paragraphs or only one paragraph.
- Extra space between paragraphs is **not** a substitute for indent in good book/magazine work (register matters); newspapers/cheap pamphlets only.
- Avoid widows (esp. page heads); early printers shortened pages to avoid them — head more noticeable than foot.
- Do not right-space last lines of paragraphs as fake indent — eye searches, white gaps disturb.

## ch-3 — Layering and Separation {#ch-3}

### Grounding trace c04 — Grid intersections that create competing negative space

- **Former candidate family / destination:** VIZ / `lexicons/interaction-ux.md`.
- **Source claim:** Tufte describes interacting lines and marks as generating extra negative-space paths that can become non-information, noise, and clutter; he recommends editing line weight and removing nonessential grids. He retains a muted grid when a graphic serves exact lookup or interpolation (printed pp.59, 61–64; extraction PDF pp.58, 60–63).
- **Observable trigger:** A quantitative display has repeated, high-contrast non-data grid or enclosure lines whose intersections create prominent white paths or patterns that visually compete with data marks.
- **Required action:** lighten or remove nonessential linework and keep only faint guides required for lookup or interpolation, because lines and gaps otherwise compete with the evidence.
- **Predicted failure if ignored:** Grid intersections and negative-space paths attract attention or imply a pattern that is not in the data.
- **Exemptions / counterexamples:** Keep faint reference lines when the task requires exact value recovery or interpolation; preserve meaningful boundaries and axes. This is not a general instruction to remove every grid.
- **Verification recipe:** Inspect the display at its intended size, identify whether lines or gaps attract attention ahead of data marks, and check whether a muted grid still supports the stated lookup task.
- **Incumbents and residual:** No surviving residual under NAME-05: a scatterplot over a dense high-contrast double-line grid with bright intersection gaps fires this recorded trigger and VIZ-12's dense-background competition trigger. Avoiding that competition resolves the grid defect. COL-09 also covers densely used rules; VIZ-10 bounds faint guides needed for absolute lookup. PERC-03 and LAY-06 are adjacent unless their own grouping or hierarchy triggers fire.
- **Disposition:** GROUNDING; not promoted (c04 retained as checked local-key trace to VIZ-12/COL-09, with VIZ-10's lookup boundary).
